drug_class: Cholinesterase inhibitor (also called an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor)
purpose: Rivastigmine is used to help manage symptoms of Alzheimer's disease and dementia related to Parkinson's disease. It does not cure these conditions, but it can help improve memory, thinking, and daily functioning. It may help slow down how quickly symptoms get worse over time.
how_it_works: Your brain uses a chemical called acetylcholine to help nerve cells communicate and support memory and thinking. In Alzheimer's and Parkinson's dementia, this chemical breaks down too quickly. Rivastigmine blocks the enzyme that breaks it down, so more of it stays available in the brain and helps nerve cells work better.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, upset stomach, dizziness, headache, and feeling tired are the most common side effects. These are often worse when starting the medication or increasing the dose. Using the patch form instead of capsules can sometimes cause fewer stomach-related side effects.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have heart problems, stomach ulcers, seizures, asthma, or kidney or liver disease before starting this medication. Do not use more than one patch at a time and always remove the old patch before putting on a new one — using too much can be dangerous. If you or a loved one notices any serious skin reactions, chest pain, fainting, or severe vomiting, contact a doctor right away.
typical_dosing: For the capsule or liquid form, treatment usually starts at a low dose of 1.5 mg twice a day with food, and is slowly increased every few weeks up to a maximum of 6 mg twice a day. The skin patch is typically started at 4.6 mg per day and may be increased to 9.5 mg or 13.3 mg per day. Your doctor will guide how and when to adjust your dose.
